_note: Verbatim rules text transcribed from CoW-Instructions.pdf (City of Winter - Rules V2, Heart of the Deernicorn, 2022). Line wrapping is joined with single spaces; the source's own spellings and typos are preserved. 'teaching' entries are the source's read-aloud text, printed in quotes.

steps.name: Introduction
steps.instruction: Take turns reading these paragraphs out loud:

substeps.name: Roleplaying
substeps.teaching: In City of Winter, we each take on the role of a different member of a family. There are many ways to roleplay. We might talk casually, like in a conversation, narrate as authors, perform as actors, or mix several styles all at once. Do whatever feels natural, or challenge yourself to try something new.

substeps.name: Group Storytelling
substeps.teaching:
As we tell the story, we sometimes step outside of our own characters to describe the world around them, what is going on, or roleplay side-characters that emerge in a scene.

We are both writers in the writing room, and fans in the audience. Feel free to converse, share ideas, or just wonder aloud about anything that interests you as we play.

substeps.name: Think small
substeps.teaching: When it is time to make something up, think small and don’t plan too far ahead. Let the story be a wondrous beast we chase but never capture. Ask questions with no clear answer, raise conflicts with no ready solution. By letting go, the story we find together will be more profound than anything we might have planned alone.

substeps.name: Safety and the X-Card
substeps.teaching: The X-Card is a safety tool. It reminds us that we all have the power to remove anything from the story that is making us feel uncomfortable, or spoiling our fun. To do so, simply tap this card, or say ‘I’d like to X card that,’ and we’ll find another way to tell our story. No questions asked.

steps.name: Choose Home & Tradition
steps.instruction: Unroll the River Scroll so that the Cloud Citadel, Rivertown, and Temple Island Locations are visible.
steps.teaching:
We begin by choosing our family’s home from these three locations. Each location has a Local Tradition indicated by the icon next to its name. This Local Tradition will be our Family Tradition.

Our options are: Lion of the Citadel, Ox of Rivertown, or Temple Heron.

steps.name: Choose Names
steps.instruction:
For this next step, everyone will need a Notecard and something to write with.

Place the Banner for our chosen Family Tradition where everyone can see it.
steps.teaching:
This is our Tradition Banner. Choose a name for your main character from this list and write it down on your Notecard.

The names list ends with a prompt you can use to make up additional names.

If you know what pronouns you’d like for your character, add those to your Notecard as well.

steps.name: Mark Age
steps.teaching:
We track our character’s age by drawing circles called Marks of Age. There is no direct correlation between the number of Marks and the exact age of a character in years. We can decide for ourselves what they mean as we play.

Choose how old you would like your character to be: Child, Youth, Parent, or Elder. Add Marks to your Notecard as follows:

Child- no Marks

Youth- one or two Marks

Parent- three, four, or five Marks

Elder- six Marks.

steps.name: Make Bonds
steps.teaching:
Our characters begin with two Bonds. A Bond represents an important relationship that helps to define your character’s role in our family.

To create a Bond, combine a prompt from the Bonds List with the name of another character and write it on your Notecard.

The prompts are organized by age, and you may only choose prompts at your age or younger.

At least one of your two Bonds must be with another main character. Your other Bond may be with a Side-Character if you wish. To create a Side-Character, choose any unused name from our Banner.

substeps.name: Choose Tradition Cards
substeps.instruction: Spread the cards from our family’s Tradition Deck (the Tradition we chose earlier) face-up on the table.
substeps.teaching:
Each main character begins with a Hand of Tradition Cards equal to their Marks of Age (Children begin with no Tradition Cards).

Holding a Tradition might mean that this tradition is important to your character, that they exemplify this tradition, or that they are somehow obligated to uphold this tradition.

Everyone can choose at once. Pick Tradition Cards that you feel drawn to. Don’t worry if you do not know what a card means when you choose it. The meaning of our traditions will naturally grow and change as we play.

substeps.name: Gather the Tradition Deck
substeps.instruction:
After we have chosen Tradition Cards, gather the remaining cards back into a deck and put it next to the River Scroll by our home.

It is not necessary to shuffle cards in City of Winter. Instead, let the order of cards naturally shift from session to session.

steps.name: Choose Tokens
steps.instruction: Place the Tokens on the table.
steps.teaching: Take a token to represent your character and place it on the picture of our home. The tokens have different images on each side. You can choose either side to represent your character, and even change sides during play if you like.

steps.name: Introduce the Umbra
steps.instruction: Have yourself or another player read the prelude from the beginning of the River Scroll.
steps.teaching: The Umbra is coming, and the Riverlands are no longer safe. Our family must flee to the City of Winter, to find another home.
steps.followUp: After the prelude is read, place the Umbra Deck next to the scroll and read the following:
steps.teachingTwo:
The Umbra represents the force that drives us from our home, and the Umbra Deck is a tool we can reach for when we want to introduce pressure or adversity into our story.

It is up to us to decide exactly what the Umbra is, and how big of a role the Umbra takes in our story as we play.

procedures.name: Tradition Scene
procedures.instruction: On your turn do the following:

steps.name: Choose a Scene
steps.instruction: Each location has several prompts called Scenes. On your turn, move your token to a scene at our family’s current location. You may choose any scene, even if another player’s token is already there.

steps.name: Share or witness?
steps.instruction: During this scene, your character will either share or witness a Tradition. Choose one of the following two options and follow the instructions:

options.name: Share a Tradition
options.instruction: Play a card from your hand, face down onto the table. (You must have at least one card in hand to choose this option.)

options.name: Witness a Tradition
options.instruction: Draw a card from either the Umbra Deck or the Local Tradition Deck (indicated by the icon next to our current location) and without looking at it, give it to another player who privately reads the prompt on the card.

steps.name: Lead the scene
steps.instruction: Describe where we are, who is there, and what is going on right now. As the scene continues, the rest of us may listen, ask questions, offer suggestions, and act out other characters.

steps.name: Pass on the Tradition
steps.instruction: Before the end of the scene, we use the chosen Tradition Card to describe how a tradition is either shared or witnessed by your character.

options.name: Share the Tradition
options.instruction: If you chose to Share a Tradition, use the prompt on your card to describe how you share a tradition with another player’s character and pass them the Card to add to their Hand.

options.name: Witness the Tradition
options.instruction:
If you are the player who has been given the Tradition Card, it is your job to look for opportunities to introduce this tradition into the scene.

Instead of roleplaying your character, roleplay as the the locals who practice this tradition. You can just describe what the people around us are doing, or, if you like, use a Banner to make up a new Side-Character.

Don’t be in a hurry. Let the scene unfold on its own, and when you’re ready, jump in and describe how the tradition is witnessed in the scene. When you are done, pass the Card to the player whose turn it is. They add it to their hand.

steps.name: End the Scene
steps.instruction: When you (the player who’s turn it is) are ready for your scene to end, let the group know. It’s now the next player’s turn.

procedures.name: Migration Scene
procedures.instruction:
Migration is when our family moves to another Location, which becomes our new Home.

At the start of your turn, if your token is already on a Scene, you may choose to play a Migration Scene. After each player has had a Migration Scene, we Migrate the Family as a group.

To play a Migration Scene, do the following:

steps.name: Why You Must Leave
steps.instruction: Place your Token on your Notecard and describe why your character knows it is time to leave.

steps.name: What You Carry
steps.instruction: If you hold more Tradition Cards than Marks of Age, decide which you will carry on the journey, and place the extras face-up on the table in front of you. These cards will remain here for now.

steps.name: Pass the turn
steps.instruction: When you are done, pass the turn. You are removed from the turn order until the rest of the players have also had their Migration Scenes. While you wait, you may still participate in other players’ turns as your main character or side-characters.

procedures.name: Migrate the Family
procedures.instruction: After each player has had a Migration Scene, we Migrate the Family as a group.

steps.name: Choose a destination
steps.instruction: We decide our destination together. We may travel to any location that is connected by a river or other path to our current location.

steps.name: What is saved
steps.instruction: If any players hold fewer cards than their character’s Marks of Age, they should look through the face-up cards that have been left behind by other players. Select cards until they hold an equivalent number to their Marks of Age. Describe how they save or preserve these traditions.

steps.name: What is Left
steps.instruction:
If unclaimed cards remain, for each remaining card, one of us must describe how this Tradition is left behind, forgotten, or practiced for the last time and discard that card.

(Discarded Tradition Cards go to the bottom of their respective Tradition Decks.)

steps.name: Migrate the family
steps.instruction:
Everyone now places their token on our destination. This becomes our new Home. There are icons next to the location names that tell us the Local Tradition. Bring this Tradition Deck and Banner into play (if it is not in play already).

Any player may resume play by taking the first turn in our new location.

procedures.name: Ending a Chapter
procedures.instruction:
At the end of each Chapter, time passes and our characters grow older.

We might end a Chapter when we near the end of our planned session, or when we reach a point in our story where we want to skip ahead in time.

When we’ve agreed to bring our current Chapter to a close, do the following:

steps.name: Mark Age
steps.instruction:
Each player adds a Mark to their character’s Notecard.

If your character is an Elder, (six Marks of Age) cross off a Mark rather than adding a Mark.

steps.name: New Bonds
steps.instruction: When your character gains a Mark, make a Bond. You may use names from our Family Tradition Banners, or any other Banner matching a Tradition Card that you hold.

steps.name: Hold Traditions
steps.instruction:
If you hold more cards than Marks of Age, choose which you would like to carry, and place the extras face-up at the center of the table.

If you hold fewer cards than Marks of Age, you may fill up your hand with any of the face-up cards.

Remaining cards are discarded.

steps.name: New Chapter or End the session?
steps.instruction: After closing a Chapter, we may begin a new Chapter if we wish. Otherwise, we end the session with a closing reflection.

options.name: Start a New Chapter
options.instruction: To start a new Chapter, everyone places their Token on our Home. Any player may take the first turn, then play continues clockwise as usual.

options.name: Closing Reflection
options.instruction:
Go around the circle and give each player space to reflect on their experience.

Some things to consider sharing:

- A moment you enjoyed

- How you are feeling right now

- An appreciation of another player

- Something you found challenging or difficult

- A moment of silence

procedures.name: New Session Setup
procedures.instruction: To start a new session in an ongoing Campaign, do the following:

steps.name: Distribute Materials
steps.instruction: Distribute the Character Notecards and Tradition Cards saved from the previous Session.

steps.name: Place Tokens
steps.instruction: Place the Tokens on the Location that was our Home in the previous Chapter.

steps.name: Start a New Chapter
steps.instruction: Any player may take the first turn, then play continues clockwise as usual. (See Death & Memory and Birth for additional, beginning-of-Chapter steps.)

procedures.name: When You Die
procedures.instruction:
If your character is an Elder (has 6 Marks), roll the Die at the start of each new Chapter.

If your roll is equal to or less than the crossed-off Marks, your character has died of old age and becomes a Memory.

When your character dies, do the following:

steps.name: Remove your Token from play
steps.instruction: Remove your token and return it to the box.

steps.name: Make a Memory Bond
steps.instruction: Make a final bond using this list:

procedures.name: Memory Scene
procedures.instruction:
For the rest of the Chapter you will play as our family’s memory of your character.

A character who is a Memory does not participate in the Migration Scene procedure or in another character’s Share a Tradition Scene.

Otherwise, continue to participate fully in other players’ turns, offering suggestions and playing side characters, or roleplaying a tradition in a Witness a Tradition Scene, as normal.

On your turn, follow the Memory Scene procedure.

steps.name: Move another Player’s Token
steps.instruction: Move another character’s Token to any scene they would normally have access to.

steps.name: Share a Tradition
steps.instruction: Choose a Tradition Card to share with this player’s character, and play it face down on the table.

steps.name: Lead the Scene
steps.instruction:
Lead the scene as you would a normal Tradition Scene, roleplaying as our memory of your character.

Roleplaying a memory could include describing something that happened long ago, how things in the scene remind us of you, or perhaps cutting away from the present moment to describe something you told us in the past.

steps.name: Share the Tradition
steps.instruction: Before the end of the scene, describe how you share your tradition and give your Tradition Card to the other player.

steps.name: Pass the Turn
steps.instruction: When you are ready for the scene to end. Let the group know, and pass the turn.

procedures.name: Birth
procedures.instruction: At the start of a new Chapter, if your character is a Memory or if you are a new player joining an existing campaign, follow these rules to make a new character:

steps.name: Choose another player
steps.instruction: Choose another player.

steps.name: Receive a name
steps.instruction: That player gives you a name. Write the name they give you on your Notecard.

steps.name: Receive a Bond
steps.instruction: The player you chose gives you a Child Bond with their character. Write down the bond they give you on your Notecard.

steps.name: Choose a Token
steps.instruction: Choose from any of the remaining Tokens to represent your character, and place it on our family’s Home.

procedures.name: Migrating to the City
procedures.instruction:
Migrating to the City introduces new rules, Traditions, and an entirely different map.

There are five entrances to the City of Winter. When we Migrate The Family to one of those entrances, we do the following:

steps.name: Remove the River Scroll
steps.instruction: Roll up the River Scroll and return it to the box.

steps.name: Remove the Umbra Deck
steps.instruction: Return the Umbra Deck to the box. If a player is holding an Umbra Tradition they may continue to do so.

steps.name: Open the City Map
steps.instruction: Unfold the City Map, and place our tokens on the location that corresponds to our Entrance. This becomes our new Home.

procedures.name: Ask Fate
procedures.instruction: When a question arises that no one wants to answer, ask Fate.

steps.name: Ask Fate
steps.instruction: Pick up the die and ask the question you want Fate to answer.

steps.name: Set Outcomes
steps.instruction:
As a group, agree to a likely, an unlikely, and a fateful outcome.

A likely outcome is the obvious result of things as they stand.

An unlikely outcome is something that could happen, but is improbable.

A fateful outcome might involve strange fortune, outside intervention, magical transformation, or new perspective.

steps.name: Fate Answers
steps.instruction:
Roll the die and describe the result:

1-3 The likely outcome

4-5 The unlikely outcome

6 The fateful outcome

rules.name: Witnessing in the City
rules.text:
Most Locations in the City have multiple Local Traditions.

When you Witness a Tradition in the City, draw one Tradition Card for each Local Tradition icon, and give all of the cards you have drawn to one other player.

rules.name: Blank Tradition Icons
rules.text: In the City, some Local Tradition icons are just blank shapes with no image. A blank icon means that each time you would draw a Tradition Card, you may choose from any of the Tradition Decks with the matching shape.

rules.name: During a scene
rules.text:
During a Witness Scene, If you are the player who received the Tradition Cards, you may now do any of the following:

- Play one Tradition Card and ignore the rest.

- Play one card first, and then later in the scene decide to play more.

- Play multiple cards together, combining prompts to describe how these Traditions have combined to create something new.

Regardless of how many Traditions you play, only pass one Tradition Card to the player whose turn it is. The rest are discarded to the bottom of their respective decks.

rules.name: City Bonds
rules.text:
If your character has at least one City Mark, you may alternately choose a prompt from the City Bonds list when making a Bond.

A City Bond represents a relationship that defines who you are and what your role is in the City.

Just like the regular Bonds List, the prompts are organized by number of Marks, and you may only choose from a list that has the same or fewer number of City Marks as your character.

rules.name: Transit Lines & Stations
rules.text: Every Location has a Transit Station that is connected to one or more Transit Lines. On your turn, whenever you Choose a Scene, you have the option to Travel to another Location.

rules.name: Travel
rules.text:
To Travel, pick up your token and describe your character’s journey. Then place your token on any Scene at your destination, and continue your turn as normal.

The total number of Stations a character can travel from Home is equal to that character’s City Marks. You may change from one Line to another mid-journey, but each change adds one to the total City Marks required for the journey.

Traveling distance is always measured from Home, even if a character’s Token is on another Location at the start of the turn.

You may include other family members in scenes at a visited location, even if they couldn’t make it there on their own.

rules.name: Migration in the City
rules.text: When we Migrate The Family, we may always choose an adjacent Location as our destination. In addition, we may Migrate to any Location that one of the migrating family members could reach through Travel with their City Marks.

rules.name: Migrate apart
rules.text:
After you’ve had your Migration Scene, you may choose to Migrate Apart instead of skipping a future turn. Characters who have also had their Migration Scene may join you if they wish. Follow the rest of the Migrate the Family procedure with the characters who chose to Migrate Apart.

Characters who are staying may Save Traditions left by characters who are leaving.

rules.name: The Wandering Borough
rules.text: The Wandering Borough is a special location that appears during a session when “The Borough Wanders” card is drawn and revealed from a Tradition Deck.

rules.name: The Borough Wanders
rules.text:
There is one copy of “The Borough Wanders” card in each of the City (diamond-bordered) Tradition Decks.

During a scene, we treat this card like a normal Tradition prompt, using it to inspire a description of the arrival of the Borough.

At the end of the scene, instead of passing the card to another player, discard it to the bottom of its deck. Place the Wandering Borough Location Card next to the edge of the map near where the scene took place. (You can put it on the map if you like, but you might have to move it if it gets in the way.)

rules.name: The Borough Leaves
rules.text:
If “The Borough Wanders” card is drawn while the Borough is already in play, the Borough now leaves. The player must describe the Borough departing at some point during the scene and then remove it from play. Any visiting character tokens are returned to their home.

Remove the Wandering Borough from play at the end of a Chapter (unless a character has made it their Home).

rules.name: Transit and The Borough
rules.text: The Borough occupies the same Station in the Transit Line as the Location where it appeared. Any character who could interact with that Location, may interact in the same way with the Wandering Borough and its Scenes.

rules.name: Living on the Borough
rules.text:
If The Wandering Borough is home to one of our characters, it remains in play from Chapter to Chapter.

At the start of each Chapter, and whenever “The Borough Wanders” card is drawn, roll the Die and consult the table below:

1. Lantern Wall

2. Smoke Street

3. Ruin Street

4. Spire Road

5. In the Pull

6. Moon Path

Choose any location along the rolled Transit Line to be the Wandering Borough’s new Location, and place it near that Location.

rules.name: Starting a New Chapter
rules.text: City of Winter is played in Chapters. During a Chapter, we take turns leading the group in a Tradition Scene. To start a new Chapter, decide who will go first then continue taking turns, clockwise.

rules.name: Starting a Campaign
rules.text:
A Campaign is the fullest way to experience City of Winter. You can start a Campaign by planning in advance, or evolve a one-shot into a Campaign by simply playing more Sessions.

Eight or more Sessions will give you a very full experience of City of Winter, though you can go much longer. Decide the number of sessions in advance, or play an open-ended campaign with no set limit.

You can also play a mini campaign with a group of friends over one long play session, or maybe over a weekend. If you fit in two or three chapters each day you should, be able to make it to the City and see a fair amount of the game.

rules.name: Storing the Game
rules.text:
Between sessions of play, store each character’s Tradition Cards next to that character’s Notecard in the box between sessions of play.

To store the City Map, fold it in half twice (hamburger-style), then fold it into thirds.

To store the River Scroll, let it hang down verticaly as you roll it up by twisting the ends of the dowel. Then, wrap the cord twice and tuck the end into the wrapping.

rules.name: Becoming forgotten
rules.text:
When you have shared your last Tradition Card, remove your Notecard from play. You may no longer take turns.

At the start of the next Chapter, follow the Birth rules to create a new character.

rules.name: Starting in the City
rules.text:
Choose your Home & Tradition from of the following options:

Moonbee of the Palace of the Moon

Fox of the Refuge

Brass Ones of Lantern Gate

Glowdog of the Dust

Crow of the Drift

Mask Maker of the Wandering Borough

optionalRules.name: The Umbra Follows
optionalRules.optionalText: By default the Umbra Deck is no longer in play when we reach the City. But your group could decide that you would like it to remain.
optionalRules.text:
Include the Umbra Deck in play with the rest of the Tradition Cards. Whenever you would draw from a Tradition Deck, you may draw an Umbra card instead.

Be aware that if you do this, the game will likely become more about the struggle against Umbra and less about the immigration experience.

optionalRules.name: Fleeing the City
optionalRules.optionalText: In this variation, we reverse the migration pattern and tell the story of a family fleeing the City to escape the Umbra.
optionalRules.text:
New Prelude

“The Umbra is coming, and the City of Winter is no longer safe. Our family must flee, to the Riverlands, to find another home.”

Escaping the Umbra

Remove the Umbra Deck from play when we reach Temple Island or Cloud Citadel.

Leaving the city

We can Migrate from the City Map to the River Scroll through any of the points of entry listed on the Riverscroll.

Some of the River Scroll prompts like “We board a lantern ship” imply a Riverlands to City journey, but I imagine your group can make that work through some slight narrative changes.

optionalRules.name: Solo Play
optionalRules.optionalText: These are rules for playing City of Winter solo. Instead of roleplaying scenes as a group, you will write scenes in a physical journal.
optionalRules.text:
Follow the normal rules of play, only instead of roleplaying scenes with a group of people, you will be writing scenes in your journal.

For each scene, choose to act as any of the main characters, moving their token and picking Tradition Cards according to the normal rules of play.

Begin every scene journal entry with the name of the main character, the name of the scene you chose, and what kind of scene it is (Tradition, Migration, Memory, etc...)

When you would Witness a Tradition, play the card onto the table and reveal it when you are ready to integrate the witnessed tradition into your scene.

optionalRules.name: Ask Fate (optional)
optionalRules.optionalText: Over the last four years, I’ve explored many ways to play City of Winter. In this section, I’ve included some ideas that I think are interesting enough to share but don’t recommend as part of the first-time experience. Try them as-is, or use them to inspire your own explorations.
optionalRules.text: When a question arises that no one wants to answer, ask Fate.

soloModules.name: Index Module
soloModules.text: The index is where you will track the information in your journal. To create your index, write index on the top left of the first page and first full spread of your journal.

soloModules.name: Main Character Module
soloModules.text:
A Main Character Module is for tracking all of the information about a single main character.

To create a new main character, turn to the first available blank spread, add that character’s name as the title of the spread, and add it to your index.

Use this space to record Marks of Age, Bonds, assigned token, character sketches, and any thoughts or reflections you have about the character.

soloModules.name: Side Character Module
soloModules.text:
The Side Character Module is for information about ALL of the side characters.

When you create a new side character, add their name to the Side Character Module. Decide how old they are, and add Marks of Age next to their name.

soloModules.name: Chapter Module
soloModules.text:
The Chapter module is where you will record your scenes along with notes, marginalia, sketches, or anything else you wish to add.

Each Chapter gets a fresh module with the Chapter number as the title. As always, number and index as you go!

guidance.label: campaign-vs-one-shot
guidance.text:
A game can last just one session. This is called a one-shot and is a great way to experience City of Winter for the first time.

During a one-shot, our group will create a family, explore their traditions of their homeland, and possibly begin our migration journey.

City of Winter may also be played as an ongoing campaign lasting many sessions.

During a campaign, we follow a family as they migrate from their home to the City of Winter, and explore how their Traditions change as generations pass.

guidance.label: learning-city-of-winter
guidance.text: If you are facilitating, familiarize yourself with these rules in advance. It’s ok to not have everything memorized, just make sure you know where to look things up when there are questions.

guidance.label: tradition-banners-in-play
guidance.text: As we travel, we will encounter different traditions. Each of the traditions we encounter has a Banner with a list of name prompts. Use these prompts to inspire other characters we meet in our story. You can keep Cards and Banners in the box when not in use.

guidance.label: keep-cards-face-down
guidance.text: Our Hands of Tradition Cards are not secret, but should be kept in hand or face-down on the table when not in use.

guidance.label: placing-a-token-on-a-location
guidance.text:
When the game asks us to place a token on our Home (or any other location), we place the token on the illustration beneath the name of that Location.

This is different from placing a Token on a Scene, which refers to written scene prompts that surround each Location.

Starting with the Tokens on the illustration, and not on the Scenes, helps us keep track of who has already taken a turn.

guidance.label: side-characters
guidance.text: While the focus of our story will be on our main characters, Side-Characters will naturally emerge through play. Everyone is welcome to describe or roleplay a side-character in a scene.

guidance.label: chapters-and-pacing
guidance.text:
We can control the pace of our story by how many Chapters we play in a session. The recommendation is to play a minimum of one Chapter per Session, but you might want to let a Chapter stretch out a couple of Sessions, depending on what is happening in your story.

If we are in the middle of the Migration Scene procedure, we must complete it before ending the Chapter.

guidance.label: side-characters-and-age
guidance.text: If you are planning to play many Chapters, track the age of Side-Characters you’ve Bonded with on your Notecard. When you start a new Chapter, you can roll for Side-Characters who are Elders, the same as you would for your main character.

guidance.label: widows-and-orphans
guidance.text:
Some of the Bonds imply that the other character is dead. You can make these Bonds with other main characters if the other player is willing. Likewise, it is okay to decide during the First-Session setup that a character is dead, and play them as a Memory for the first chapter.

When this happens, they still receive Traditions during the Hold Tradition step, as normal.

guidance.label: other-ways-to-die
guidance.text:
Sometimes it makes sense in the story for your character to die. Perhaps something comes up in a scene, or you just feel like it is time.

Whatever the case, you always decide what happens to your main character; this includes death.

guidance.label: leaving-mid-game
guidance.text: If a player ever needs to leave a campaign or session in-progress, transition their character to a side character and add their Tradition Cards to the pool next time we Migrate the Family or end a Chapter.

guidance.label: ending-a-campaign
guidance.text:
City of Winter does not have a pre-planned end goal. The stories of our characters end when they die, but the story of our family can continue for as long as we wish to explore it.

When the group is ready for the Campaign to end, open up the river scroll and remember our family’s journey as part of the Closing Reflection after the last Session.

guidance.label: rejoining-as-children
guidance.text: As we play City of Winter, we create a world that is unique to our game. By joining our campaign as a Child, the new player experience aligns with the experience of their character who is also new to our world.

guidance.label: role-juggling
guidance.text: Juggling lots of roles in one scene can be a challenge. If possible, it is best not to ask a player to roleplay both the local traditions and their own character in the same scene.

guidance.label: different-homes
guidance.text: While living apart, Migration mechanics affect each group separately. For example, you can Save Traditions left by a family member only if they currently share a Home.

guidance.label: fate-advice
guidance.text:
- If someone has a good idea for what should happen, just go with that, no need to roll.

- Outcomes should drive the story forward.

- If you’re not interested in something happening in the story, don’t set it as an outcome.

- Go a little deeper than just failure or success to drive the story forward. What are the consequences of that failure or success?

- When setting a Fateful Outcome, don’t be afraid to think big!

guidance.label: plan-for-a-longer-setup
guidance.text: The City is a lot to take in all at once. Ten Tradition Decks, transit mechanics, and prompts that are more weird and abstract. The River Scroll gives us a chance to slowly ease into the world with more familiar fantasy themes and mechanics that build bit by bit. If you are running a City game for new players, expect to spend more time explaining the city mechanics.

guidance.label: bullet-journaling
guidance.text: The method of journaling presented here is adapted from Ryder Carroll’s “Bullet Journal” method.

guidance.label: adding-a-module
guidance.text:
Whenever you add more modules to your journal, turn to the next available blank spread and add the title of that module to the top left corner, number the pages, and enter it into your index.

Always give yourself a minimum of 1 full spread (2 pages)for each new module.

guidance.label: extending-a-module
guidance.text: If you run out of space in a module, turn to the next blank spread in your journal and continue the module there, indexing as you go.

guidance.label: promoting-a-side-character
guidance.text: At the end of a Chapter, you may promote a side character to a main character. To do this, create a new Main Character Module and transfer your Side-Character’s information to the module.

guidance.label: combined-play
guidance.text:
You can mix solo and group play.

Inviting a guest

Invite another player as a guest for a session of your solo game.

During scenes, assign them the role of side characters, or ask them to take on the role of the locals during your Witness scenes.

Assign them characters and roles for parts of the story that you don’t know much about so they have space to create without worrying about conflicting with your backstory.

Breaking off of a group Campaign

You could break off a part of an existing group campaign as a solo campaign. Perhaps use this as a way to develop the story of a side character who was left behind, or explore what happened in the years between Chapters of your campaign.

guidance.label: journal-setup
guidance.text: I recommend choosing a journal with an elastic band and a couple of bookmarks.

guidance.label: solo-first-session
guidance.text: I recommend just creating one main character for the first session and letting things grow organically from there. This character, and the two side characters they are Bonded with, will be your starting characters in the story.

guidance.label: solo-holding-traditions
guidance.text: Between sessions of play, tuck Traditions held by this character into the pages of their Main Character Module.

guidance.label: by-ship-or-by-caravan
guidance.text:
Some Locations have two versions depending if we are traveling by Caravan or by Lantern Ship.

The Lantern Ship route is indicated by a dashed line and a Lantern Ship icon. The Caravan route is indicated by a Caravan icon and a blue line.

Make sure you are on the page for the correct version when you Migrate to these Locations.

guidance.label: moving-character-tokens-in-the-city
guidance.text:
In the City, you will find it necessary to flip through the Atlas frequently as we explore different Locations on our turns.

When your campaign gets to this point, it is better to place your Token next to the Atlas rather than on the Atlas when choosing a Scene. This allows us to pick up the Atlas and change Locations without having to disturb the other player’s tokens.
